newsitem.title: DUBAI: FEATURE-Dubai braces for promotion blitz.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Dubai braces for promotion blitz.

text.p: Armies of Asian labourers are hanging discount signs, decorations and five million coloured lights on street lamps in the Gulf Arab emirate of Dubai for a month-long shop-until-you-drop festival.
Officials hope the festival which starts on Thursday will promote the city's image as the Gulf's trade and tourism centre.
Hotels, the local airline, restaurants and a dozen shopping malls announced a wide range of discounts after the government began a global publicity blitz to lure shoppers and tourists.
Officials in the small oil-producing emirate, which hosts scores of conferences and exhibitions each year, hope the festival will draw up to two million shoppers.
Dubai, one of seven emirates that make up the United Arab Emirates, has stepped up efforts in recent years to diversify its economy by promoting trade, industry, tourism and services.
It is hoping that tourism revenue will match its oil income by the year 2000.
SUPERLATIVES ABOUND
Officials are calling the month-long retail extravaganza "the greatest shopping festival on earth". Superlatives abound.

They expect the city to turn over $1 billion-worth of business during the fiesta, which will also include bazaars, raffle draws, fireworks, art exhibitions, sports events, and international dance and theatre troupes.
Festival chief executive Mohammed al-Gergawi said 3,000 retailers had been screened ... "to ensure quality and give value for shoppers". Discounts of up to 70 percent are on offer.
Dubai's first shopping festival last year lured 1.5 million people, mostly from neighbouring Gulf Arab states, the Middle East, the Indian subcontinent and Europe.
They spent $800 million on such luxuries as gold, carpets, electronics, textiles and computers. Some shoppers complained that prices were relatively high even after discounts.
"Dubai will be promoted as a shopping haven for the whole region ... from east to west and from north to south," Gergawi said.
"It is not just for shopping, but also a cultural, sporting and entertainment extravaganza for the whole family and we want people to come and enjoy themselves".

Organisers travelled to new Asian markets like Thailand, Singapore and Malaysia, in search of more shoppers and improved on last year's displays, setting up what they say is the world's largest carpet bazaar and a 300-shop computer zone.
CHARACTERS FROM DISNEY WORLD IN DUBAI

Characters from Disney World in Orlando, Florida, will stage 12 musical nights at a city park and 100 street performers flown in from around the world will entertain children in malls and on a main street cleared of traffic.
Raffle prizes include 61 kg (134 lb) of gold and 101 Japanese Lexus cars.
Gergawi said the festival would also help Dubai's ambition to replace Singapore as the world's largest distributor of gold. Last year's "Dubai city of gold" theme had already paid off.
"Last year, we were number two after Singapore in terms of gold distribution in the world, and this year we expect to be number one," he said.
The World Gold Council, a non-profit association, said in January that Dubai, with gold imports of 350 tonnes in 1996 was neck-and-neck with Singapore, which imported 357 tonnes.
MOST OF DUBAI'S GOLD IMPORTS ARE RE-EXPORTED
Most of the gold imported into Dubai is re-exported to the Indian subcontinent, the world's single largest gold market.

Gold traders in Dubai's covered old souk said they hoped the shopping event would attract big buyers of jewellery and investment bars. They said this could help improve the market, in which recent higher international prices have suppressed local demand.
"Our eyes are on the festival and the potential it might get us," said one trader. "Gold pieces in Dubai cater for all tastes and cultures and prices are at their lowest now."
Dubai's airline Emirates has reduced fares on incoming flights and offered passengers extra luggage allowance so they can take more shopping home.
